E-VERIFY — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Alex Lee · Acme Corp

ABOUT THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet describes E-Verify, a federal electronic employment eligibility verification system operated by the U.S. Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS), and California's specific statutory restrictions on an employer's use of it, in connection with Acme Corp's employment of Jordan Alex Lee with a start date of October 1, 2026. E-Verify is a separate system from, though it draws information from, the Form I-9 employment eligibility verification process that federal law requires for every new hire; this sheet does not restate the Form I-9 requirements themselves, which are addressed in a separate information sheet. This document is not the Form I-9, does not enroll Acme Corp in E-Verify or submit any query to it, and does not state, verify, or determine Jordan Alex Lee's actual identity, employment authorization, or immigration status.

WHAT E-VERIFY IS AND ITS LEGAL BASIS
E-Verify is an internet-based federal program, administered by DHS/USCIS, that allows an enrolled employer to electronically confirm the employment eligibility of a worker against Social Security Administration and DHS records. It traces its legal basis to a set of federal "pilot programs of employment eligibility confirmation" that Congress established in 1996 as Subtitle A of Title IV of Division C of the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act (IIRIRA), codified as a note under 8 U.S.C. § 1324a rather than as freestanding numbered sections of the U.S. Code. One of those three original pilot programs was itself named the "E-Verify Program" and was later expanded to all 50 states; California's own Labor Code separately confirms that the electronic system it regulates traces to this same 1996 federal enactment, renamed "E-Verify" in 2007.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "The Secretary of Homeland Security shall conduct 3 pilot programs of employment eligibility confirmation under this subtitle."
  — Pilot Programs for Employment Eligibility Confirmation, Pub. L. 104-208, div. C, title IV, subtitle A, § 401(a) (set out as a note under 8 U.S.C. § 1324a) (uscode.house.gov text), U.S. Code, statutory note under 8 U.S.C. § 1324a, establishment of pilot programs (https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-prelim-title8-section1324a&num=0&edition=prelim)
  "This includes the Basic Pilot Program, enacted by Section 404 of Public Law 104-208 and renamed in 2007 as the E-Verify Program, and other pilot programs for electronic employment eligibility confirmation."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 2813(a) (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text), California Labor Code, definition of "electronic employment verification system" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=2813.&lawCode=LAB)
  Known gap: This is federal and California law, used as real evidence of E-Verify's identity as a federal pilot-program system and its statutory point of origin — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs any reader's situation, and not a claim about any specific individual's actual work authorization status. The federal citation below is to a statutory note set out under 8 U.S.C. § 1324a (Pub. L. 104-208, div. C, title IV, subtitle A, as subsequently amended), not to numbered subsections of § 1324a itself — this note-versus-codified-section distinction matters because a note is set out by the Office of the Law Revision Counsel as historical/uncodified text rather than as the operative U.S. Code section, even though it remains legally operative. Separately, this clause's drafter found, in the course of reading that note, that the pilot programs' nominal sunset date has been repeatedly extended by later appropriations-related public laws that amend only the sunset date (most recently to September 30, 2026, by Pub. L. 119-75, div. I, § 5014, enacted Feb. 3, 2026) rather than by any permanent reauthorization — an honest, undisclosed-until-now gap in the premise that E-Verify's authorization is settled or permanent: as of this clause's checked date, the current extension is due to lapse September 30, 2026, absent a further extension. The California citation is to Cal. Lab. Code § 2813(a), a definitions provision from a different jurisdiction than the federal citation, so the two are independent sources of each other, not the same source viewed twice.

E-VERIFY USE IS VOLUNTARY FOR MOST EMPLOYERS, WITH FEDERAL-GOVERNMENT EXCEPTIONS
As a general federal rule, participation in E-Verify is voluntary: an employer may elect to use it, but the federal government may not require an employer to participate, except in specifically enumerated categories. The statutory note establishing the program identifies its own carve-outs from that voluntary default, including a requirement that each department of the federal executive branch elect to participate. Whether a particular non-federal employer instead falls under a mandatory-use category — such as the federal-contractor mandate described in a separate clause of this information sheet, or a state-law mandate — is a separate question this general voluntariness rule does not resolve.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Except as specifically provided in subsection (e), the Secretary of Homeland Security may not require any person or other entity to participate in a pilot program."
  — Pilot Programs for Employment Eligibility Confirmation, Pub. L. 104-208, div. C, title IV, subtitle A, § 402(a) (set out as a note under 8 U.S.C. § 1324a) (uscode.house.gov text), U.S. Code, statutory note under 8 U.S.C. § 1324a, voluntary election (https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-prelim-title8-section1324a&num=0&edition=prelim)
  "Each Department of the Federal Government shall elect to participate in a pilot program and shall comply with the terms and conditions of such an election."
  — Pilot Programs for Employment Eligibility Confirmation, Pub. L. 104-208, div. C, title IV, subtitle A, § 402(e)(1)(A)(i) (set out as a note under 8 U.S.C. § 1324a) (uscode.house.gov text), U.S. Code, statutory note under 8 U.S.C. § 1324a, federal executive department exception (https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-prelim-title8-section1324a&num=0&edition=prelim)
  Known gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence of E-Verify's default voluntary status and of the existence of specific federal-government exceptions to it — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs any reader's situation, and not a claim about whether any particular reader's employer falls into a mandatory-use category. Both citations below are to different subsections of the same statutory note (Pub. L. 104-208, div. C, title IV, subtitle A, § 402) — subsection (a) (the general voluntariness rule) and subsection (e)(1)(A)(i) (the federal-executive-department exception); they are treated as one source, not independent, disclosed together here rather than presented as though they corroborate each other from separate origins. This clause does not attempt to catalog every category the note lists in subsection (e) — it also covers the legislative branch and certain parties already found to have violated federal immigration-related employment law under a formal order — and states only the general shape of the exception, not its full scope.

MANDATORY E-VERIFY USE FOR CERTAIN FEDERAL CONTRACTORS
Federal acquisition regulations require an employer awarded a covered federal contract to enroll in and use E-Verify, both for its new hires generally and for employees specifically assigned to the contract, and to flow the same requirement down to certain subcontractors. This requirement is implemented through a standard clause that a contracting officer must insert into qualifying solicitations and contracts above a stated dollar threshold, subject to stated exceptions (including contracts performed entirely outside the United States, short-duration contracts, and certain purchases of commercial off-the-shelf items). Whether Acme Corp holds a contract that includes this clause, and is therefore subject to this mandate, is a separate question this clause does not resolve.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "This subpart prescribes policies and procedures requiring contractors to utilize the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), United States Citizenship and Immigration Service's employment eligibility verification program (E-Verify) as the means for verifying employment eligibility of certain employees."
  — 48 C.F.R. § 22.1800 (eCFR, current as displayed 2026-09-02), Federal Acquisition Regulation, employment eligibility verification, scope (https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-48/chapter-1/subchapter-D/part-22/subpart-22.18)
  "Insert the clause at 52.222-54, Employment Eligibility Verification, in all solicitations and contracts that exceed $150,000, except those that—"
  — 48 C.F.R. § 22.1803 (eCFR, current as displayed 2026-09-02), Federal Acquisition Regulation, instruction to insert the E-Verify contract clause (https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-48/chapter-1/subchapter-D/part-22/subpart-22.18)
  "begin to use E-Verify to initiate verification of employment eligibility of all new hires of the Contractor, who are working in the United States, whether or not assigned to the contract, within 3 business days after the date of hire"
  — 48 C.F.R. § 52.222-54(b)(1)(ii) (eCFR, current as displayed 2026-09-02), Federal Acquisition Regulation, Employment Eligibility Verification clause, verification of new hires (https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-48/chapter-1/subchapter-H/part-52/subpart-52.2/section-52.222-54)
  Known gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence of a specific, currently codified category of employer for whom E-Verify use is mandatory rather than voluntary — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs any reader's situation, and not a claim about any specific employer's own contract status. This clause's drafter traced the mandate to its currently codified regulatory text, in the Federal Acquisition Regulation (FAR) at 48 C.F.R. §§ 22.1802-22.1803 (agency policy and the instruction to insert the contract clause) and 48 C.F.R. § 52.222-54 (the clause itself, in its January 2025 form as reflected in the eCFR). The FAR text itself states that this requirement rests on "[s]tatutes and Executive orders" generally, without citing a specific executive order by number in the subpart text this clause read; this clause's drafter is aware, from general background knowledge rather than from a citation verified against a primary source in this research pass, that the commonly cited executive-order lineage for the federal-contractor E-Verify mandate is Executive Order 12989 (1996) as amended by Executive Order 13465 (2008), but did not independently fetch and verify the text of either order against a primary source in this research pass (an outbound fetch to a federal-register source was blocked in this environment) — so that specific EO citation is disclosed here as unverified background, not asserted as verified. The two FAR citations below are to different parts of the FAR (subpart 22.18 and the standalone clause at 52.222-54); they are independent regulatory citations, not two views of the same provision.

CALIFORNIA RESTRICTION ON A STATE OR LOCAL AGENCY MANDATING E-VERIFY
Under California law, except as required by federal law or as a condition of receiving federal funds, neither the state nor a city, county, city and county, or special district may require an employer to use an electronic employment verification system such as E-Verify — including as a condition of a government contract, as a condition of obtaining or keeping a business license, or as a penalty for a licensing violation.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "neither the state nor a city, county, city and county, or special district shall require an employer to use an electronic employment verification system, including under the following circumstances"
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 2812 (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text), California Labor Code, prohibition on state or local mandate of an electronic employment verification system (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=2812.&lawCode=LAB)
  Known gap: This is California law, used as real evidence of a specific statutory restriction on California state and local government agencies (not on private employers directly) — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs any reader's situation, and not a claim about whether any specific state or local requirement a particular employer may separately encounter is, in fact, an unlawful E-Verify mandate under this section. This section, Cal. Lab. Code § 2812, restricts what government bodies may require of an employer; it is a distinct provision from Cal. Lab. Code § 2814, addressed in separate clauses of this information sheet, which instead restricts what an employer may do with E-Verify on its own initiative. This clause corrects a plausible mis-citation: the state/local-mandate prohibition is codified at § 2812, not at § 2814.

CALIFORNIA RESTRICTION ON AN EMPLOYER'S OWN USE OF E-VERIFY
Separately from the restriction on government mandates, California law makes it unlawful for an employer to use E-Verify to check the employment authorization status of an existing employee, or of an applicant who has not yet been offered employment, at a time or in a manner not required under federal law or authorized under a federal E-Verify memorandum of understanding — except as required by federal law or as a condition of receiving federal funds. The same California statute makes clear that this restriction does not prohibit an employer from using E-Verify, in accordance with federal law, to check a person who has already been offered employment.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "it shall be unlawful for an employer, or any other person or entity to use the federal electronic employment verification system known as E-Verify to check the employment authorization status of an existing employee or an applicant who has not been offered employment at a time or in a manner not required under subsection (b) of Section 1324a of Title 8 of the United States"
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 2814(a)(1) (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text), California Labor Code, restriction on employer use of E-Verify for existing employees and pre-offer applicants (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=2814.&lawCode=LAB)
  "Nothing in this section shall prohibit an employer from utilizing the federal E-Verify system, in accordance with federal law, to check the employment authorization status of a person who has been offered employment."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 2814(a)(2) (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text), California Labor Code, post-offer use of E-Verify not prohibited (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=2814.&lawCode=LAB)
  Known gap: This is California law, used as real evidence of a specific statutory restriction on an employer's own, self-initiated use of E-Verify — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs any reader's situation, and not a claim about whether any particular employer's use of E-Verify would in fact fall outside what federal law requires or a governing E-Verify memorandum of understanding authorizes (a fact-specific question this clause does not resolve). Both citations below are to different paragraphs of the same statutory subsection, Cal. Lab. Code § 2814(a) — paragraph (1) (the restriction) and paragraph (2) (the post-offer carve-out) — and are treated as one source, not independent, disclosed together here rather than presented as though they corroborate each other from separate origins.

CALIFORNIA NOTICE REQUIREMENT UPON A TENTATIVE NONCONFIRMATION
California law requires that, upon using E-Verify to check a person's employment authorization status, if the employer receives a tentative nonconfirmation from the Social Security Administration or DHS indicating the information entered did not match federal records, the employer must comply with the notification procedures required under the governing E-Verify memorandum of understanding, and must furnish to the employee any notification issued by the Social Security Administration or DHS containing information specific to that employee's E-Verify case, or any tentative nonconfirmation notice, as soon as practicable.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "The employer shall furnish to the employee any notification issued by the Social Security Administration or the United States Department of Homeland Security containing information specific to the employee’s E-Verify case or any tentative nonconfirmation notice."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 2814(b) (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text), California Labor Code, notice of tentative nonconfirmation (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=2814.&lawCode=LAB)
  Known gap: This is California law, used as real evidence of a specific statutory notice requirement tied to E-Verify use — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs any reader's situation, and not a claim about whether any specific individual has received or will receive a tentative nonconfirmation. The statute ties the substance of the required notification procedures to a separate federal document (the E-Verify memorandum of understanding) rather than specifying those procedures itself; this clause's drafter did not independently fetch or verify the current text of that memorandum of understanding in this research pass, and discloses that as an honest gap rather than describing its contents.

CALIFORNIA CIVIL PENALTY FOR AN UNLAWFUL USE OF E-VERIFY
California law makes an employer that violates this E-Verify restriction liable for a civil penalty of up to $10,000 for each violation, in addition to other available remedies, and treats each unlawful use of E-Verify on an employee or applicant as a separate violation. The same statute states that this section is intended to prevent discrimination in employment, not to sanction the potential hiring or employment of a person not authorized to work under federal law.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "an employer who violates this section is liable for a civil penalty not to exceed ten thousand dollars ($10,000) for each violation of this section. Each unlawful use of the E-Verify system on an employee or applicant constitutes a separate violation."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 2814(c) (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text), California Labor Code, civil penalty for a violation (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=2814.&lawCode=LAB)
  Known gap: This is California law, used as real evidence of the specific civil-penalty mechanism this statute creates for a violation of the employer-use restriction described in a separate clause of this information sheet — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs any reader's situation, and not a claim about any specific employer's actual liability. This clause's drafter read the full text of Cal. Lab. Code § 2814 and found this civil penalty, capped per violation, to be the only enforcement mechanism the statute itself states; the statute does not, in the text this clause's drafter reviewed, create an explicit private right of action naming who may bring an action to recover the penalty or specifying an enforcing agency, and this clause does not assert that either exists.

RELATIONSHIP TO THE FORM I-9 PROCESS AND E-VERIFY TIMING
E-Verify draws on information an employee and employer already recorded on Form I-9, but it is a separate system layered on top of the mandatory I-9 process, not a substitute for it, and California's own statutory definition expressly excludes the Form I-9 itself from the category of "electronic employment verification system" it regulates. Where E-Verify use applies — such as under the federal-contractor mandate described elsewhere in this information sheet — federal contracting rules require the E-Verify query for a new hire to be initiated within a set number of business days of the date of hire, on a timetable distinct from the separate Form I-9 completion deadline addressed in this office's I-9 information sheet.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "The term “electronic employment verification system” does not include the I-9 Employment Eligibility Verification form or any other employment eligibility systems that are required by federal law."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 2813(a) (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text), California Labor Code, Form I-9 excluded from the definition of an electronic employment verification system (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=2813.&lawCode=LAB)
  "begin to use E-Verify to initiate verification of employment eligibility of all new hires of the Contractor, who are working in the United States, whether or not assigned to the contract, within 3 business days after the date of hire"
  — 48 C.F.R. § 52.222-54(b)(1)(ii) (eCFR, current as displayed 2026-09-02), Federal Acquisition Regulation, Employment Eligibility Verification clause, verification timing for new hires (https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-48/chapter-1/subchapter-H/part-52/subpart-52.2/section-52.222-54)
  Known gap: This clause draws on both federal regulatory law and California statutory law, used as real evidence that E-Verify and Form I-9 are legally distinct, and of one specific, currently codified E-Verify timing rule — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs any reader's situation, and not a claim about any specific individual's hire date or the Form I-9 deadline (addressed in a separate document). The "3 business days after the date of hire" figure quoted in the federal-contractor-mandate clause of this information sheet is codified, for federal contractors specifically, at 48 C.F.R. § 52.222-54(b)(1)(ii) — a regulation, not a statute. This clause's drafter was unable to independently verify, against a primary source, whether an identical or different business-day timing rule applies to E-Verify participants generally (that is, non-federal-contractor employers who elect to use E-Verify voluntarily): outbound fetches to e-verify.gov and uscis.gov, which would ordinarily carry the E-Verify memorandum of understanding and User Manual describing that general timing rule, were blocked in this environment, and this clause does not assert a specific timing figure for that broader population beyond what the FAR text itself establishes for federal contractors. The Form I-9 timing deadline itself (three business days of hire, with a same-day exception for very short hires) is addressed with its own citations in a separate I-9 information sheet clause (id: i9_verification_timing) and is not re-derived here.

E-VERIFY PARTICIPATION DECLARATION
Acme Corp states its E-Verify participation status with respect to Jordan Alex Lee's employment as follows: voluntary participant. If Acme Corp's use of E-Verify is mandatory rather than voluntary, the basis for that mandate is: federal contract clause under 48 C.F.R. 52.222-54. This declaration states Acme Corp's own participation status and does not itself determine, for any other employer, whether E-Verify use is mandatory or voluntary, which depends on facts about that employer described elsewhere in this information sheet.

ACKNOWLEDGMENT
By signing below, the undersigned acknowledge that this information sheet was provided and that it states general rules of federal and California law about the E-Verify program rather than advice about Jordan Alex Lee's specific situation or Acme Corp's specific legal obligations.

Employer: Acme Corp
By: _______________
Date: _______________

Employee: Jordan Alex Lee
Signature: _______________
Date: _______________

citations.cite: California Labor Code, prohibition on state or local mandate of an electronic employment verification system
citations.quote: neither the state nor a city, county, city and county, or special district shall require an employer to use an electronic employment verification system, including under the following circumstances

expectedJSON.gap: This is California law, used as real evidence of a specific statutory restriction on California state and local government agencies (not on private employers directly) — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs any reader's situation, and not a claim about whether any specific state or local requirement a particular employer may separately encounter is, in fact, an unlawful E-Verify mandate under this section. This section, Cal. Lab. Code § 2812, restricts what government bodies may require of an employer; it is a distinct provision from Cal. Lab. Code § 2814, addressed in separate clauses of this information sheet, which instead restricts what an employer may do with E-Verify on its own initiative. This clause corrects a plausible mis-citation: the state/local-mandate prohibition is codified at § 2812, not at § 2814.

expectedJSON.body: Separately from the restriction on government mandates, California law makes it unlawful for an employer to use E-Verify to check the employment authorization status of an existing employee, or of an applicant who has not yet been offered employment, at a time or in a manner not required under federal law or authorized under a federal E-Verify memorandum of understanding — except as required by federal law or as a condition of receiving federal funds. The same California statute makes clear that this restriction does not prohibit an employer from using E-Verify, in accordance with federal law, to check a person who has already been offered employment.

citations.cite: California Labor Code, restriction on employer use of E-Verify for existing employees and pre-offer applicants
citations.quote: it shall be unlawful for an employer, or any other person or entity to use the federal electronic employment verification system known as E-Verify to check the employment authorization status of an existing employee or an applicant who has not been offered employment at a time or in a manner not required under subsection (b) of Section 1324a of Title 8 of the United States

citations.cite: California Labor Code, post-offer use of E-Verify not prohibited
citations.quote: Nothing in this section shall prohibit an employer from utilizing the federal E-Verify system, in accordance with federal law, to check the employment authorization status of a person who has been offered employment.

expectedJSON.gap: This is California law, used as real evidence of a specific statutory restriction on an employer's own, self-initiated use of E-Verify — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs any reader's situation, and not a claim about whether any particular employer's use of E-Verify would in fact fall outside what federal law requires or a governing E-Verify memorandum of understanding authorizes (a fact-specific question this clause does not resolve). Both citations below are to different paragraphs of the same statutory subsection, Cal. Lab. Code § 2814(a) — paragraph (1) (the restriction) and paragraph (2) (the post-offer carve-out) — and are treated as one source, not independent, disclosed together here rather than presented as though they corroborate each other from separate origins.

expectedJSON.body: California law requires that, upon using E-Verify to check a person's employment authorization status, if the employer receives a tentative nonconfirmation from the Social Security Administration or DHS indicating the information entered did not match federal records, the employer must comply with the notification procedures required under the governing E-Verify memorandum of understanding, and must furnish to the employee any notification issued by the Social Security Administration or DHS containing information specific to that employee's E-Verify case, or any tentative nonconfirmation notice, as soon as practicable.

citations.cite: California Labor Code, notice of tentative nonconfirmation
citations.quote: The employer shall furnish to the employee any notification issued by the Social Security Administration or the United States Department of Homeland Security containing information specific to the employee’s E-Verify case or any tentative nonconfirmation notice.

expectedJSON.gap: This is California law, used as real evidence of a specific statutory notice requirement tied to E-Verify use — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs any reader's situation, and not a claim about whether any specific individual has received or will receive a tentative nonconfirmation. The statute ties the substance of the required notification procedures to a separate federal document (the E-Verify memorandum of understanding) rather than specifying those procedures itself; this clause's drafter did not independently fetch or verify the current text of that memorandum of understanding in this research pass, and discloses that as an honest gap rather than describing its contents.

expectedJSON.body: California law makes an employer that violates this E-Verify restriction liable for a civil penalty of up to $10,000 for each violation, in addition to other available remedies, and treats each unlawful use of E-Verify on an employee or applicant as a separate violation. The same statute states that this section is intended to prevent discrimination in employment, not to sanction the potential hiring or employment of a person not authorized to work under federal law.

citations.cite: California Labor Code, civil penalty for a violation
citations.quote: an employer who violates this section is liable for a civil penalty not to exceed ten thousand dollars ($10,000) for each violation of this section. Each unlawful use of the E-Verify system on an employee or applicant constitutes a separate violation.

expectedJSON.gap: This is California law, used as real evidence of the specific civil-penalty mechanism this statute creates for a violation of the employer-use restriction described in a separate clause of this information sheet — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs any reader's situation, and not a claim about any specific employer's actual liability. This clause's drafter read the full text of Cal. Lab. Code § 2814 and found this civil penalty, capped per violation, to be the only enforcement mechanism the statute itself states; the statute does not, in the text this clause's drafter reviewed, create an explicit private right of action naming who may bring an action to recover the penalty or specifying an enforcing agency, and this clause does not assert that either exists.

expectedJSON.body: E-Verify draws on information an employee and employer already recorded on Form I-9, but it is a separate system layered on top of the mandatory I-9 process, not a substitute for it, and California's own statutory definition expressly excludes the Form I-9 itself from the category of "electronic employment verification system" it regulates. Where E-Verify use applies — such as under the federal-contractor mandate described elsewhere in this information sheet — federal contracting rules require the E-Verify query for a new hire to be initiated within a set number of business days of the date of hire, on a timetable distinct from the separate Form I-9 completion deadline addressed in this office's I-9 information sheet.

citations.cite: California Labor Code, Form I-9 excluded from the definition of an electronic employment verification system
citations.quote: The term “electronic employment verification system” does not include the I-9 Employment Eligibility Verification form or any other employment eligibility systems that are required by federal law.

citations.cite: Federal Acquisition Regulation, Employment Eligibility Verification clause, verification timing for new hires
citations.quote: begin to use E-Verify to initiate verification of employment eligibility of all new hires of the Contractor, who are working in the United States, whether or not assigned to the contract, within 3 business days after the date of hire

expectedJSON.gap: This clause draws on both federal regulatory law and California statutory law, used as real evidence that E-Verify and Form I-9 are legally distinct, and of one specific, currently codified E-Verify timing rule — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs any reader's situation, and not a claim about any specific individual's hire date or the Form I-9 deadline (addressed in a separate document). The "3 business days after the date of hire" figure quoted in the federal-contractor-mandate clause of this information sheet is codified, for federal contractors specifically, at 48 C.F.R. § 52.222-54(b)(1)(ii) — a regulation, not a statute. This clause's drafter was unable to independently verify, against a primary source, whether an identical or different business-day timing rule applies to E-Verify participants generally (that is, non-federal-contractor employers who elect to use E-Verify voluntarily): outbound fetches to e-verify.gov and uscis.gov, which would ordinarily carry the E-Verify memorandum of understanding and User Manual describing that general timing rule, were blocked in this environment, and this clause does not assert a specific timing figure for that broader population beyond what the FAR text itself establishes for federal contractors. The Form I-9 timing deadline itself (three business days of hire, with a same-day exception for very short hires) is addressed with its own citations in a separate I-9 information sheet clause (id: i9_verification_timing) and is not re-derived here.
